en: The dream you saw has come true:
The maiden sovereign seeks you—
No such thing has happened in an age.
When you face one whose beauty blooms like a bazaar,
Could anyone confronting you survive?
A fairy maiden has come for your happiness.
While alive, every brave young man
Dreams of taking a beauty as his bride.
A maiden fairer than a fairy has come,
And among mortals none is like you.
The true spirit of your mighty father Manas
Has given you its aid.
May your fortune and happiness unfold;
Before you, mighty warrior,
May the light of God shine forth.
Nothing like this has existed in the world;
Your forefather Manas leads you,
And his spirit gives you aid.
Though you dig from it, it never runs out—
A treasure-house of amassed wealth is there.
There, play will satisfy your longing;
There are games and laughter there,
And the renowned beauty, the skilled maiden, is there.
When you meet her, she will sate your affection;
The renowned maiden Bermet is there.”
So Akjoltoy spoke,
Telling a thousand different tales,
And uttering words of wondrous delight.
When Akjoltoy had spoken,
Kulansur’s head could not be turned,
And the grey wolf could not remain merely watching.
From father and forefather
Came the wings he inherited for his people;
To be drawn toward women
Had been his custom from the beginning.
The noble warrior, upheld by the spirits,
When he heard this news,
Took on a thousand different airs.
Lion-hearted Seytek grew impassioned;
Whatever your elder, hero Akjoltoy,
Told him early already seemed too late.
To behold the radiant poor maiden,
To gaze upon her face,
His two eyes became four with longing.
His precious soul cried out,
His heart grew hot and his body melted,
Longing to plunge into pleasure,
To lie upon a narrow bed,
To eat meat from a single bowl,
And meet her face-to-face in tenderness,
To play until his desire was sated,
And surrender himself to passion.
His heart surged and his eyes shone,
As though he might never reach her;
He boiled with impatient haste.
Yet he could not leave Joltoy behind,
Nor could he abandon the poor, troubled man
And pass him by upon the road.
The noble warrior, mindful of honor,
That noble man like a towering mountain,
With eyes reddening like fire,
Grew gaunt in frantic haste,
And sank into sorrow and regret;
His heart turned toward his beloved,
And he withdrew alone.
Now Joltoy understood his impatience.
His elder kinsman Akjoltoy
Stepped into the golden-soled stirrup
And sprang astride his horse.
Leading his companion Seytek,
He raced across the open country;
Kulansur and Kulunsur
Rode with their stirrups clashing.
To the lowlands of the Op River,
An immense and mighty stream,
Along the banks of Keng-Özön,
The grey wolves came at last.
They were travelers upon a campaign,
Their souls blazing and burning.
Full of cunning and fierce in wrath,
They stood apart from other men;
They would yield to all the world for none,
Illustrious heroes mighty in spirit.
Those who saw them thought them Mount Kap,
And those who grappled with them met ruin.
Grey wolves of singular splendor,
True lion-hearted heroes,
Their majesty mountainous, their wrath severe—
Those who fought them were laid low.
Wearing out their horses as they scouted the land,
They took on a thousand fearsome airs.
Seeing the maidens, they grew excited;
The champions who had never seen such girls
Lost all composure,
And rode forward with great bounding strides,
As though they might trample everything down,
Striking panic into every living soul.
Those who stood and watched them
Were left bewildered and distracted;
Their majesty was like a tiger’s menace,
And they looked ready to seize their prey.
The unfortunate fairy maiden,
Of wondrous and cutting discernment,
Experienced from seeing many things,
Was exceedingly astute and capable;
She had reckoned the world a thousand ways,
And had seen the shrewdest maidens.
Resourceful and richly endowed with wisdom,
Eloquent in speech and mistress of words,
She was accomplished and outstanding.
She had set sentries upon the heights,
Stationing them there by magic,
And guards stood at her gate.
The unfortunate sovereign lady
Was ringed about by an iron fence,
With only one road by which to enter;
So vast was her wealth.
A grove of plane trees encircled it.
A fortress wall encircled it.
In its center stood a golden throne,
With a garden of fortune and wealth,
And a keeper tending it.
There were trained warriors there,
And a thousand greater than those warriors,
There were men armed with heavy muskets,
And if an order came from Bermet,
There were marksmen who never missed.
There were those who answered the instant she spoke,
Born and bred for that purpose.
Gripping clubs as large as houses,
Giants guarded her gate.
Her champions stood ready,
And she had peoples of many kinds.
The ill-fated fairy maiden
Had fortified herself thus.
She had not stood idly by,
But gathered champions from among the fairies.
The reason she gathered champions
Was that if he were a hero and a lion,
One who could subdue the whole world,
If he were truly a gray-maned hero,
If his fortune were complete,
If his heart were broad as a lake,
If he were an unflinching lion,
Then all the champions
He would trample underfoot like charcoal.
But if he were a man without courage,
With a cowardly, feeble heart,
Then at the sight of the champions,
He would find nowhere to hide,
And no grave into which to crawl,
He would squander all his riches,
And flee back in panic.
If he were a lion of supreme courage,
He would stride on unconcerned,
Regarding not merely the champions, but the world itself
As no more than the hem of his robe,
And would march straight in.
The prudent, ill-fated Bermet
Thought deeply and devised a plan,
And arranged many wondrous trials.
From the city of the fairies
She gathered champions and brave men,
Heroes and lions,
And fortified herself securely;
She had not remained idle.
She thus tested the valor
Of Seytek, who would come to face her.
When he saw the champions,
He did not rein aside his steed,
Nor falter and halt,
But his eyes blazed like a lion’s,
And he fiercely ground
His broad, gate-like teeth.
He loaded his white musket,
And when he showed his wrath, he thundered,
Until the black earth, hairy-breasted,
Seemed shaken to its depths.
Six grooms brought up their horses,
And these six, led by Akjoltoy,
Rode freely at the very front.
When they saw these six,
The champions and guards,
Those who watched the approaches,
Despaired of their precious lives.
Those valiant lions upheld by the saints
Appeared before the simpletons’ eyes
Like angels of death.
The guards scattered in a frantic rush,
Bursting away in every direction,
Separating one by one instead of massing together.
Then it became clear that lion Seytek,
The gray-maned hero, was truly a lion.
The champion guards at the gate
Each seemed worth a thousand, they said,
Yet they were left utterly bewildered.
All the champions crowded together,
Clasping their hands to their breasts,
And marveled at brave Seytek.
Unable to withstand his fury,
With no soul able to resist his courage,
The guards dared not face him;
They could not come near
The face of valiant Seytek, the gray-maned hero.
His terrible presence threw every soul into panic.
Upon two thoroughbred steeds,
Seytek and Akjoltoy
Made their horses trample
The splendid carpets spread before them.
The six grooms who tended the horses
And the companions beside them
Were tigers, each worth a thousand men.
By the splendor of their array,
They were all keen-eyed warriors
Fit to subdue the whole world.
Each bore a spear,
And if you looked at some of them,
They wore unsheathed swords at their sides.
The tigers formed a ring,
All keen-eyed warrior companions,
Men who would not flee
When black muskets cracked.
If an overwhelming enemy host came,
They were warriors who never panicked.
When a fierce gun barked,
They served without flinching.
If some other disaster came,
If their frail lives were endangered,
They stood beneath the banner.
They were steadfast gray-maned heroes,
Fierce in presence and mighty in wrath,
Who laid every opponent low.
The guards beheld their terrible presence,
And from the force of their wrath
Several met their doom and died,
Merely on seeing the gray-maned hero’s form.
Their minds reeled.
The guards standing watch
Ran about in confusion,
Despairing of their precious lives,
Losing their senses and growing weak,
Overwhelmed by his terrible presence.
They rushed about in panic
And beat the great war drum.
To the hapless fairy maiden,
Bewildered and nearly senseless,
They now brought the news:
“I have seen men of surpassing splendor;
I could not go and face them—
Every one is a champion, a crimson flame.
If roused, they could tear the soul from the body,
And if they drew a breath, it seemed
They could suck down all eighteen thousand worlds.
I saw a lion of magnificent stature,
A hero beyond all measure.
I despaired when I saw his terrible presence;
